Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Notes: POC weekly check-in focused on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and streaming tradeoffs, kernel choices for long sequences, and next steps for the pilot.

Summary:
- Reviewed last week's TTFT numbers from Redwood Dedicated vs hosted fallback; discussed outliers and cold-start variance.
- Agreed on a short kernel selection matrix to test quantized int8 vs fused attention kernels for 2k+ seqs.
- Action items assigned for runbook, prompt uploads, and scheduling bench.

Topics:
- TTFT variability and cold-start paths
- Streaming chunk sizes and early flush heuristics
- Sequence length distribution and KV cache pressure
- Kernel choice (fused vs strided attention) and quantization tradeoffs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Marcus Lee (Redwood AE): ok hey everyone thanks for joining on a Wednesday, we'll try to keep this tight, um Nina and I will run through the perf numbers and then we want to align on next kernel tests and the peering window with Tom.
[00:18] Priya Desai (Aurea): thanks Marcus, excited to see the TTFT results, last week we saw some big spikes in the morning traffic so want to understand root cause.
[00:35] Nina Rao (Redwood SE): cool, quick frag — I'm going to share screen, got the CSVs up. So two baseline runs: hosted route (redwood api) and dedicated pool with pinned gpu config. First token latencies reported as p50/p95/p99 — note we have a couple of outliers where p99 hit 360ms.
[00:55] Elena Martinez (Aurea): yep we saw same, but sometimes it's 450ms on cold starts which surprised us, we thought dedicated would be more stable.
[01:12] Marcus Lee: right, so the big thing is cold-start vs warm-requests — our dedicated pool has warm workers but if the KV cache hasn't seen that prompt prefix there's still fetch and compile heh, and sometimes the kernel selection path falls back to a safe kernel which increases TTFT.
[01:33] Tom Wilkes (Aurea SRE): can you unpack the "compile" bit? our infra team is worried about jitter from JITs or runtime kernel swaps.
[01:45] Nina Rao: yeah totally. Runtime does a lightweight kernel probe at first few tokens to decide fused attention vs strided kernels; if sequence length is uncommon (we saw 1536-2048 ranges) it picks a path that compiles a specialized kernel, that compile step can add 80-120ms on the first request. We normally pre-warm but if traffic pattern is bursty you get a cold worker that hasn't compiled yet.
[02:12] Priya: so is the compile happening on the GPU or CPU? can it be precompiled?
[02:20] Nina: compile hooks are GPU-side (PTX/CUDA kernels) and the runtime ships prebuilt kernels for the common configs, but the combinatorial space of seq-len x batch x model-variant means we don't have every single one prebuilt. We can precompile the top 6 shapes for Aurea's workload if you share token distribution.
[02:44] Elena: we'll do that, I'll upload token histograms.
[02:50] Marcus: great, that'll cut the p99 significantly. We also noticed streaming chunk sizes matter — if you flush every token you have small batches; if you accumulate 16-32 token chunks you amortize overhead.
[03:08] Samir Khan (Aurea Product): for interactivity we can't add large delay, 16 tokens sounds acceptable, anything larger hurts UX.
[03:18] Nina: yeah 16 is a good trade; also early-flush heuristics: send partial frames when there's low beam or deterministic output.
[03:28] Priya: what about prefix caching? our chat flows have a 250-token system prompt repeated across many users.
[03:35] Nina: prefix/KV cache is huge — we saw 30-40% savings on token compute when KV cache hit; but that relies on consistent encoding and pinned workers. If queriers hit different shards, you lose those savings.
[03:50] Tom: does Redwood shard by customer or by session? we saw cache misses when traffic comes from multiple regions.
[03:58] Marcus: we shard by worker pool with session affinity when you enable sticky routing; we recommended enabling session affinity for your use case. That keeps KV cache locality.
[04:12] Tom: ok we'll test sticky routing in staging.
[04:20] Nina: another noisy factor is quantization path — int8 is faster at token time but sometimes models show slight regression on certain evals; we saw TTFT improvements of ~20% with q8 but also occasional degeneracy on long-completions.
[04:38] Elena: can you show the eval diffs?
[04:42] Nina: sure opening the eval sheet — for 2k seq completions q8 had a small BLEU-ish drop on our rerank tests, not massive but noticeable. We recommend running quality tests against your exact prompts.
[05:00] Priya: we'll do that, quality is priority for our customer flows.
[05:07] Marcus: on kernel choices — we're proposing a short matrix: test fused attention (high throughput fused kernels), strided attention (memory-friendly for >2k), and tiled kernels for narrow batch shapes. We'll run each with and without q8.
[05:25] Samir: timeline? we need results for an internal milestone in 10 days.
[05:30] Nina: we can run an automated bench across the cluster in 48 hours once we get the prompt sets and token distro. The heavy part is the precompile phase for the uncommon shapes which takes a few hours but can be parallelized.
[05:45] Priya: what about streaming latency improvements we saw when you change the early-flush to 8 tokens — that seemed to reduce user perceived TTFT but increased overall token cost because of inefficiencies.
[05:58] Marcus: correct — early flush reduced perceived TTFT by ~35ms p50 because users saw output earlier, but it increased total tokens 2-3% due to partial framing and repeated overhead. It's a business tradeoff.
[06:15] Elena: for our pilot we'd prioritize perceived latency for demo users but keep cost bounds for production. So maybe we enable early-flush for canary and monitor cost.
[06:25] Nina: good plan. We'll include a cost delta in the bench results.
[06:32] Tom: question on VPC and peering: we need a maintenance window to add the peering for dedicated testing, what's required from our side?
[06:40] Marcus: mostly a short firewall rule update and route acceptance, it's a 15 minute window; Tom we put an action item for you to confirm the exact time.
[06:49] Tom: noted.
[06:52] [07:00] Jonah Patel (Redwood Support): quick nuance — when we enable session affinity we sometimes see hotspotting on a worker, so we mix affinity with soft-balancing to avoid overloading a single GPU. That can slightly increase TTFT variance but avoids throughput cliffs.
[07:15] Priya: thanks, that helps.
[07:20] Marcus: ok next I want to call out two surprising outliers in the crawl — one was a driver bug where the runtime copied a small host-side buffer synchronously adding ~120ms; we pushed a patch in the dedicated image rolled last night. If you're on the older dedicated image you'll still see that.
[07:40] Elena: we're on the older image, we'll update.
[07:44] Nina: update note: if you switch image do a rolling restart and watch KV warmup.
[07:52] [08:00] Priya: on the bench results can you include breakdown per route and per token (model vs infra) so we can present to execs?
[08:08] Marcus: yes we'll include token-level breakdown and a short slide for execs.
[08:14] Samir: any competitor notes to be aware of? we tried Vertex in a side experiment and the quick TTFT was good but the streaming semantics were trickier.
[08:27] Nina: yes we noted Vertex's prewarm model is aggressive but costs more; Anthropic had better deterministic streaming semantics in our tests but lower throughput on long sequences. We'll add a short row in the matrix.
[08:40] Tom: on instrumentation — can Redwood surface token-level traces to our APM? we need to correlate spikes to infra.
[08:48] Jonah: we emit per-request timing spans and you can hook them into X-Ray/Datadog; we'll share the tracing docs.
[08:56] Priya: perfect.
[09:00] Marcus: ok let's recap decisions: Aurea will share token histograms and three representative prompt sets; Redwood will run kernel matrix with and without q8, precompile top shapes, and include cost/quality deltas; we'll test sticky routing and early-flush in canary.
[09:18] Elena: agreed.
[09:22] Marcus: any blockers?
[09:24] Tom: just the peering window and we need the maintenance time.
[09:28] Priya: none from product.
[09:30] Marcus: cool. We'll schedule kernel bench for next Tuesday and I'll send the runbook.
[09:36] [09:45] (crosstalk) all: thanks everyone.
